subject: biology
title: How plants store sunlight
lead: Plants turn light into stored chemical energy.
body: In photosynthesis, chlorophyll absorbs light in a plant's chloroplasts. The plant uses that energy to combine water and carbon dioxide into sugars. Oxygen is released as a by-product. The sugars supply energy and building material for growth.
takeaway: Light + water + carbon dioxide → sugar + oxygen.
question: What does a plant make during photosynthesis?

subject: physics
title: Why the sky looks blue
lead: Air scatters some colors of sunlight more than others.
body: Sunlight contains a range of visible wavelengths. Molecules in the atmosphere scatter shorter blue wavelengths more strongly than longer red wavelengths. Blue light therefore reaches us from many directions across the daytime sky. At sunset, sunlight passes through more air, so much of the blue has scattered away before it reaches you.
takeaway: The same scattering explains blue skies and many red sunsets.
question: Which visible wavelengths scatter more strongly in the atmosphere?

subject: history
title: How Roman roads handled rain
lead: Many Roman roads were built with a raised center and sloping sides.
body: Road builders packed several layers of stone and gravel to make a durable surface. The center often sat slightly higher than the edges, allowing rainwater to run into roadside drains. A connected road network helped move goods, officials, soldiers, and messages across the Roman world.
takeaway: A road's shape can be as important as the materials beneath it.
question: Why raise the center of a road?
options: To let water drain toward the sides
To make carts travel faster uphill
To mark the edge of a province

subject: math
title: Prime numbers as building blocks
lead: Every whole number greater than one can be factored into primes.
body: A prime number has exactly two positive factors: one and itself. Twelve is not prime because it can be divided by two, three, four, and six. Its prime factorization is 2 × 2 × 3. Prime factorization gives each positive whole number a unique set of prime building blocks, apart from their order.
takeaway: The number 1 is not prime; it has only one positive factor.
question: Which is the prime factorization of 18?

subject: environment
title: Where ecosystem energy begins
lead: Most food webs begin with energy captured from sunlight.
body: Plants and algae use photosynthesis to store light energy in sugars. Herbivores obtain some of that energy by eating producers, and predators obtain some by eating other animals. At each transfer, organisms use much of the energy for life processes and release it as heat. This is why food chains usually have fewer top predators than producers.
takeaway: Energy flows through ecosystems; nutrients can cycle through them.
question: What is the main energy source for most food webs?

subject: psychology
title: Why recalling helps learning
lead: Trying to retrieve an idea strengthens practice with that memory.
body: When you try to recall information without looking at your notes, you practice finding that information in memory. This is called retrieval practice. Research in learning science finds that retrieval practice can improve later recall, especially when you check your answer and revisit material over time. Rereading can feel fluent without showing what you can remember independently.
takeaway: Read a short section, close it, explain the idea, then check what you missed.
question: What is retrieval practice?
options: Trying to recall information without looking

subject: astronomy
title: The Moon is moving away
lead: The Moon's average distance from Earth increases by a few centimeters each year.
body: The Moon raises tides on Earth. Because Earth rotates faster than the Moon orbits, the tidal bulge is carried slightly ahead of the Moon. Its gravity transfers a small amount of orbital energy to the Moon, gradually widening the orbit. Lunar laser ranging measurements find an average recession of about 3.8 centimeters per year.
takeaway: This change is slow and measurable; it does not mean the Moon is about to leave Earth.
question: What transfers energy to the Moon's orbit?
options: The gravity of Earth's tidal bulge

subject: art
title: Why ultramarine was precious
lead: Natural ultramarine pigment was made from the blue stone lapis lazuli.
body: For centuries, lapis lazuli mined in regions of Central Asia was traded over long distances. Grinding the stone produced a vivid blue pigment called ultramarine. Its scarcity and cost meant patrons sometimes specified where artists should use it. Synthetic ultramarine became available in the nineteenth century, making the color less expensive.
takeaway: Art materials can reveal trade routes, technology, and patronage.
question: What was natural ultramarine made from?

subject: language
title: Singular they has a long history
lead: English speakers have used “they” for an unspecified person for centuries.
body: In a sentence such as “Someone left their umbrella,” they and their refer to one person whose identity is not specified. Writers have used this construction for hundreds of years. Many people also use they/them pronouns for themselves. Using the pronouns someone asks you to use is a direct way to refer to them respectfully.
takeaway: Context tells you whether “they” refers to one person or more than one.
question: In “Someone left their umbrella,” how many people does “their” refer to?

subject: computer-science
title: How internet packets travel
lead: Data is divided into packets that can travel across different network routes.
body: Internet protocols divide many kinds of data into packets. Packets carry addressing information so routers can forward them toward their destination. They may take different routes and are reassembled at the receiving end. If packets are missing or arrive out of order, transport protocols can help detect and correct the problem.
takeaway: Packet switching lets networks route pieces of data flexibly.
question: What do routers use to forward packets?

subject: economics
title: A simple supply and demand model
lead: A market price can respond to how much buyers want and sellers offer.
body: In a basic competitive-market model, demand describes how much buyers are willing to purchase at different prices, while supply describes how much sellers are willing to offer. The price where the two quantities match is called the equilibrium price. Real markets can be affected by many other factors, so this model is a starting point rather than a complete explanation.
takeaway: A model clarifies one mechanism; it does not describe every real-world detail.
question: In the basic model, what does equilibrium mean?
options: Every buyer pays a different price

subject: geography
title: Why continents move
lead: Earth's outer shell is divided into moving tectonic plates.
body: The lithosphere, Earth's rigid outer layer, is broken into plates that move slowly over the softer, hotter mantle beneath. Their motion is driven by forces including slab pull and mantle flow. Where plates meet, they can move apart, collide, or slide past one another. These boundaries are associated with many earthquakes, volcanoes, and mountain ranges.
takeaway: Plate motion is usually only a few centimeters per year.
question: What is Earth's rigid outer layer called?

subject: literature
title: How conflict gives a story shape
lead: A story's central tension gives characters something to respond to.
body: In narrative, conflict can arise between characters, within a character, or between a character and forces such as society or nature. Conflict creates questions for the reader: what will the character choose, and what will it cost? It does not have to mean a fight. A difficult decision or competing goal can provide the pressure that moves a plot forward.
takeaway: Look for the goal, the obstacle, and the choice a character makes.
question: Which can create narrative conflict without a physical fight?

subject: philosophy
title: What makes an argument valid
lead: Validity is about whether a conclusion follows from its premises.
body: An argument is valid when there is no possible case in which all its premises are true and its conclusion is false. Validity does not guarantee that the premises are actually true. A sound argument is valid and also has true premises. Separating these two checks helps evaluate reasoning clearly.
takeaway: Check the structure of an argument separately from the truth of its premises.
question: What makes an argument sound?
options: It is valid and its premises are true

subject: civics
title: Why governments divide power
lead: Separation of powers assigns government responsibilities to different branches.
body: In the United States federal system, legislative, executive, and judicial powers are assigned to different branches. Each branch has defined responsibilities, and checks and balances give them ways to limit or review some actions of the others. The details come from the Constitution, laws, and court interpretations. The design aims to prevent power from accumulating unchecked.
takeaway: Separation and checks are related safeguards, but they are not the same mechanism.
question: What is one purpose of checks and balances?
options: To let branches limit or review some actions
To give every branch identical duties
To remove the role of courts

subject: music
title: How rhythm organizes sound
lead: Rhythm is the pattern of sounds and silences over time.
body: A beat is a regular pulse listeners can feel or tap. Rhythm arranges notes and rests in relation to that pulse, often grouping beats into measures. Tempo describes how fast the beat moves. A piece can keep the same tempo while changing its rhythm, creating a new pattern without speeding up.
takeaway: Beat is the pulse; rhythm is the pattern played around it.
question: What does tempo describe?

subject: chemistry
title: Why cell membranes are selective
lead: The cell membrane controls what enters and leaves a cell.
body: Cell membranes are made largely of a phospholipid bilayer. Its interior repels many water-soluble substances, while membrane proteins provide channels or carriers for particular molecules and ions. This selective permeability helps cells maintain internal conditions. Some molecules cross by diffusion; others require energy or transport proteins.
takeaway: A membrane is an active boundary, not a simple wall.
question: What can membrane proteins do?

subject: health
title: How cues shape habits
lead: A repeated cue can make a behavior easier to remember.
body: A habit often forms when a behavior is repeated in a stable context. A cue — such as finishing breakfast or arriving home — can prompt the behavior. Making a desired behavior easy to start and connecting it to a reliable cue can support consistency. Habits vary between people, and missing one day does not erase prior practice.
takeaway: Choose a clear cue and a behavior small enough to repeat.
question: What is a cue in a habit loop?
options: A signal that prompts a behavior
A reward that must be expensive

subject: design
title: How contrast guides attention
lead: Differences in size, color, or weight can show what matters first.
body: Visual contrast helps people distinguish elements and establish hierarchy. A large heading beside smaller body text signals a difference in role. Strong contrast can improve readability, especially between text and background. Too many competing contrasts, however, make a page feel noisy, so designers reserve the strongest treatment for the most important information.
takeaway: Use contrast to clarify priority, then keep secondary elements quieter.
question: Why should the strongest contrast be used selectively?
options: So the most important information stands out
So every element looks equally important
To make text harder to read

subject: writing
title: Make sentences easier to follow
lead: A sentence is easier to read when its subject and action are clear.
body: Readers use a sentence's subject and verb to understand who is doing what. When several ideas compete for the main clause, the action can become hard to find. Try stating the main point first, then add context or qualifications. This does not mean every sentence must be short; it means each sentence should make its relationships easy to follow.
takeaway: Find the main subject and verb, then check that the sentence says what you intend.
question: What is one useful revision check?
options: Can I identify the main subject and action?
Can I replace every verb with a noun?
